title: Points in Polygon Helper: Inside or Outside?
description: Test whether points fall inside a polygon with the Points in Polygon Helper — ray-casting point-in-polygon checks for lists of coordinates. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, the test point 40.7832, −73.9666 falls inside a drawn four-corner parcel while 40.7580, −73.9855 falls outside it — two verdicts from one ray-casting pass each.
quick_answer: The Points in Polygon Helper tests whether coordinate points lie inside a polygon — the point-in-polygon question behind geofencing, service areas and jurisdiction checks. Supply the polygon and the points and read an inside or outside verdict for each, computed by ray casting.
steps_intro: Cast a ray, count the crossings — odd is in, even is out:

body.t: Is this customer inside the delivery polygon? The verdict list is the operations answer — drawn zones from the
family get audited here point by point.
A spreadsheet of sites claims a county; test the coordinates against the county polygon and the impostors confess. At scale this is a GIS join; for a list, it is this page.
School zones, tax districts, conservation areas — when the question is one point and one boundary, the helper answers without a GIS installation.
Ray casting is the undergraduate classic: cast a horizontal ray, count edge crossings, odd means inside. Testing your own implementation against this page is the homework's honest mirror.

Against a four-corner test parcel (corners near 40.7663–40.8001 N, −73.9762 to −73.9570 W): the centre point 40.7832, −73.9666 is inside — any ray crosses once. Times Square's 40.7580, −73.9855 is outside — it sits south-west of every corner.

A point exactly on an edge is the algorithm's philosophy exam: floating-point geometry rarely lands exactly on, but surveyed points can. The helper reports boundary points as their own verdict rather than flipping a coin — check its note for the convention in force.

popular_table.title: How the verdict is reached
rows: A ray leaves the test point in a fixed direction (usually east)
Each polygon edge the ray crosses adds one
Vertices and boundary points follow a stated convention — never luck
popular_table.note: The method works for any simple polygon, concave included — the parcel with a bite taken out is where naive bounding-box tests fail and ray casting earns its keep.

faq: A closed ring of coordinates in order — the boundary the points are tested against. Self-intersecting rings produce meaningless verdicts; keep the boundary simple, as with area measurement.

Reported under a stated boundary convention (commonly counted as inside for geofencing, or flagged separately). For legal boundary questions, only the survey decides — the helper flags the case rather than ruling on it.
A courtyard or exclusion zone is a hole ring: points inside the hole are outside the effective polygon. Supply the hole ring where the tool accepts one; otherwise test and invert manually.
Latitude, longitude — this site's convention. Longitude-first lists are the classic silent failure: the polygon lands in the ocean and every verdict is 'outside', correctly and uselessly.
At parcel and city scales the planar test is exact enough; continental polygons deserve spherical point-in-polygon, which the geodesy tools discuss. Match the method to the polygon's size.
Lists here; databases and GIS spatial joins at industrial scale. The verdicts must agree — spot-check the industrial output against this page's first principles.
Test each polygon in turn; a point's membership is per-polygon, and overlaps are possible where zones overlap. The helper keeps the questions separate so the answers stay true.
Why not use a bounding box?
Boxes are the fast pre-filter, not the verdict: a concave polygon's box contains much outside ground. Ray casting is the verdict the box only advertises.
